Md. Matiur Rahman
Vs.
Md. Iman Ali @ Md. Imam Miah & others
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.:-  This appeal by special leave is from a judgment and order of the High Court Division dated January 18, 1979, passed in Civil Revision No. 14 of 1978, dismissing an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, on setting aside the concurrent decisions of the lower appellate court and the trial court, simply on the ground that the pre-emptor did not adduce evidence that the quantity of laid sought to be pre-empted which added to the total quantity of land already held by him would not exceed the ceiling prescribed by section 90 of the said Act. 

 2. Appellant had filed the application in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Tangail seeking pre-emption of '28 cents of land out of '69 cents of land comprised in C.S. Plot No. 548/782 of which he is a co-sharer, transferred to respondent No. 1 under a sale deed dated June 6, 1970 without serving any notice of the transfer upon him. The application was resisted by respondent No. 1, the pre-emptee, taking the ground that it was barred by limitation and that he brought about improvement of the land at a cost of Tk. 500/-. The trial court on evidence rejected both the grounds and allowed the pre-emption by an order dated April 26, 1976. An appeal preferred by the pre-emptee was dismissed by the Subordinate Judge, whereupon the pre-emptee made a revisional application under section 115, Civil Procedure Code before the High Court Division where for the first time a ground was taken that the application for pre-emption was liable to be dismissed as the pre-emptor did not fulfill the requirements of section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in that no evidence was led to show that the maximum ceiling of land i.e. 100 standard big has, would not be exceeded if the land pre-empted be added to the quantity of land already held by him for himself and his family. Contention of the pre-emptor that he hardly held 10 big has of land and that there was a genuine omission to adduce evidence to this effect, particularly when no objection was raised by the pre-emptee, was rejected by the High Court Division. A prayer was made for remand to lead evidence on this question but it was also rejected; orders of both the courts below were set aside and the application for pre-emption itself was dismissed under the impugned order of the High Court Division. 

 3. Leave was granted to consider the question whether it is incumbent upon the court to record a finding keeping in view the requirement of section 90 as to whether pre-emption if allowed would contravene section 90 even when no objection was raised by the pre-emptee. Section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that no person shall be entitled to purchase or otherwise acquire any quantity of land which added to the total quantity of land already held by him exceeds one hundred standard big has. And section 96 of the said Act provides, among other things, that no co-sharer tenant or a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred shall have right to pre-emption unless he is a person to whom transfer of a holding or portion thereof can be made under section 90. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division relying upon a decision of the Dacca High Court in Satya Ranjan Haldar v. Surendra Nath Das (1) as well as on his own decision in a previous case, namely Nayeb Ali v. Akhtar Rahman (2) held that it is for the pre-emptor to adduce evidence that the ceiling set forth in section 90 will not be contravened if the pre-emption is allowed and that the court must record a finding to this effect. It may be mentioned here that on this very question there is another decision by the High Court Division in the case of Abdur Rahman v. Baser Ali (3) in which it has been held that where there has been no averment made by the pre-emptee as to the pre-emptors claim that if the pre-emption is allowed provision of section 90 will not be contravened the application for pre-emption cannot be dismissed. In the instant case this decision was not referred to by the learned Single Judge. 

 4. On consideration of the decisions referred to above it is found that facts of these cases are quite distinguishable from one another. In the case reported in 13 DLR, 338, the preemptor claimed that he did not hold any quantity of land which together with the land sought to be pre-empted would not exceed the ceiling. A written objection was raised by the pre-emptee challenging the claim, but no evidence was led by the pre-emptor to prove his claim. A Division Bench observed that the trial court should not have allowed the pre-emtption without establishment of the fact that the pre-emptor was a person to whom transfer could be made under section 90. In the case reported in 29 DLR 153, there was an assertion in the application for pre-emption that the ceiling of 100 standard bighas would not be exceeded if the pre-emption is allowed, but no objection was raised by the pre-emptee whereupon the pre-emption was allowed by the trial court without, however, recording a finding that the pre-emptor was entitled to pre-emption on the basis of section 90. The learned Single Judge set aside the pre-emption on an application under section 115 C. P. Code. In the instant case the pre-emptor did not adduce evidence that the quantity of land sought in be pre-empted, when added to the land already held by him, would not exceed the ceiling. No objection was raised by the pre-emptee either in the trial court or in the lower appellate court where the application was resisted on other grounds, and it is for the first time during the hearing of the revisional application that the question was raised. The pre-emptee even did not take it as a ground in his revisional application. The pre-emptor made a prayer for remand stating that he hardly got in his possession 10 bighas of land and that he would adduce evidence to supply the omission. The learned Single Judge has observed that the courts below erred in the exercise of the jurisdiction in overlooking the statutory requirements of section 90 and that "an important decision of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court presided over by the then Chief Justice should not have been overlooked". There is no dispute that a person seeking pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act must show that he is a person entitled to purchase or acquire land within the maximum ceiling as set out in section 90. But mere omission to make an assertion in his application or to adduce evidence to this effect, in the absence of any averment to the contrary, will not render the application liable to be dismissed. If no objection has been raised at any stage of the trial the pre-emptor should be given an opportunity to lead evidence on this point when question is raised. Similarly, omission to record a finding to this effect in such a circumstance cannot be a ground for dismissal of the pre-emption case but the omission should be supplied, if necessary, calling for evidence. This is quite different from a case where no evidence is led in spite of objection having been raised, as the case of 13 DLR already referred to.
